name: SPIDriver
firmware_note: Single fixed firmware; not user-reflashable with alternate firmware. Open BSD-licensed hardware/firmware/host tools.
price_note: $29.00 direct from spidriver.com (official vendor site). Adafruit sells it at $29.95; Lab401 lists it around EUR-converted $34.95-37.80 as a EU reseller.
skill_note: Conceptually simple (one protocol, a live display of what's on the wire) but you still need to understand SPI framing and chip-select behaviour to use it productively.
build_note: Bare open-hardware PCB, no case. Plug in over USB and drive it from the GUI, CLI or Python bindings - nothing to solder.
summary: A dedicated single-protocol SPI bus probe: a small open-hardware board built around an FTDI USB-serial chip and a Silicon Labs EFM8 controller, with a built-in display that shows live SPI traffic, voltage and current as you probe a target. Adafruit's own listing describes it as 'kinda like a Bus Pirate with a display and great Python support.' It is the SPI-only sibling to the I2CDriver from the same maker.
honest_take: This is a narrower, more expensive way to talk to SPI devices than a Bus Pirate or a $5 FTDI/CH552 adapter - the entire value proposition is the live display and the clean host tooling (GUI, CLI, Python/C bindings), not raw capability. 500 Kbps sustained SPI is fine for flash chips and sensors but slow next to a real logic analyzer or a dedicated SPI programmer, and it has zero debug-port (JTAG/SWD) or I2C support - buy the I2CDriver or a Bus Pirate 5 if you need those too. If you already own a Bus Pirate or a Glasgow, this adds nothing you don't have; it earns its keep specifically for people who want a purpose-built, always-on SPI monitor on the bench rather than a general multi-protocol tool.
best_for: Watching live SPI traffic on the bench while developing a driver
Dumping/writing SPI flash with clean host-side tooling
A dedicated always-connected SPI monitor separate from a general debug tool
not_for: High-speed SPI capture - 500 Kbps sustained is slow next to a real logic analyzer
Any protocol other than SPI - buy the I2CDriver or a Bus Pirate instead
JTAG/SWD debugging - it has no debug-port support at all

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Exact EFM8 part number not published by the vendor or by Adafruit's reseller listing. Paired with a standard FTDI USB-serial adapter chip for the host link.
hardware.gpio: SPI signals plus two auxiliary GPIO (A/B), two GND, two 3.3 V and two 5 V power outs, all color-coded; signals are 3.3 V and 5 V tolerant
notable_physical: Built-in 3.3 V and 5 V target power supplies with current monitoring
Color-coded jumper wiring
Live display of bus state, uptime and running CRC of traffic

spi_flash_dump.note: Core function; sustained SPI transfers at 500 Kbps with onboard 3.3/5 V power for the target.

logic_analyzer.note: Live color display of SPI signal lines and traffic on the device itself, plus a running CRC, but this is a protocol monitor, not a general-purpose multi-channel logic analyzer with buffered capture.

i2c.note: SPI only. The I2CDriver is the equivalent product for I2C.

jtag_swd.note: No debug-port support of any kind.

glitching.note: No fault-injection hardware - it is a passive/active bus probe, not a glitcher.

scriptable.note: GUI, command-line, and C/C++ and Python 2/3 host bindings provided for Windows, Mac and Linux.

standalone_untethered.note: Host-tethered over USB; the display shows state but the device does not operate without a host driving it.

app_store.note: No companion mobile app or app catalog - desktop GUI/CLI/library only.

web_ui.note: No web-based interface; control is via desktop GUI, CLI or the Python/C bindings.

sd_logging.note: No storage on the device; all data is streamed live to the connected host.

legal.notes: A passive bench probe with no radio - legal to own and use everywhere. As with any bus probe, reading data off a device you do not own or lack authorization to inspect can raise anti-circumvention (DMCA 1201) or computer-misuse issues depending on jurisdiction; this is about the target, not the tool.

name: I2CDriver
firmware_note: Single fixed firmware; open hardware/firmware/tools under BSD license.
price_note: $29.00 direct from i2cdriver.com. Adafruit sells it at $29.95; Lab401 lists it around $35 as a EUR-converted reseller price. A cheaper I2CMini variant also exists from the same maker for a stripped-down single-port version.
skill_note: Straightforward to wire up (three ready-made ports with jumpers included) but you still need to understand I2C addressing, pull-ups and clock stretching to interpret what it shows you.
build_note: Bare open-hardware PCB, no case. Three sets of color-coded jumpers included; no soldering.
summary: The I2C-only counterpart to the SPIDriver: a small open-hardware USB probe with a live display of bus traffic (including a live address map of every device it sees on the bus), programmable auto-tuning pull-up resistors, and three identical I2C ports so you can probe several devices without rewiring. Built around the same FTDI + Silicon Labs EFM8 combination.
honest_take: The programmable, auto-tuning pull-up resistors are the genuinely useful part - getting pull-up values wrong is a classic source of flaky I2C bugs, and this tool removes the guesswork, as does the live address map that shows every device answering on the bus. But like the SPIDriver, it is a single-protocol tool at multi-protocol-tool pricing: a Bus Pirate 5 costs roughly twice as much but adds SPI, UART and 1-Wire on top of I2C, and this device has zero JTAG/SWD or SPI capability of its own. Buy this specifically if I2C is most of your bench work and you want the nicest possible I2C-only experience, not as a general hardware-hacking tool.
best_for: Debugging flaky I2C buses where pull-up values are suspect
Probing multiple I2C devices at once via the three ports
Clean, well-documented host tooling for driver development
not_for: Any protocol other than I2C
JTAG/SWD debugging
Hobbyists who want one tool that does everything - see Bus Pirate 5 instead

hardware.gpio: Three identical I2C ports, each with power and I2C signal lines; 3.3 V output, all 5 V tolerant
notable_physical: Three color-coded I2C ports with jumpers included
Programmable, auto-tuning I2C pull-up resistors
Live display of bus state, address map, uptime and running CRC

logic_analyzer.note: Live graphical display of I2C signal lines and decoded traffic on the device itself, not a general multi-channel capture tool.

spi_flash_dump.note: I2C only - see the SPIDriver for SPI.

scriptable.note: GUI, command-line, and C/C++ and Python 2/3 host bindings for Windows, Mac and Linux.

name: TermDriver 2
firmware_note: Runs standard CircuitPython under the hood; firmware and PCB design are open source (BSD 3-clause) and field-upgradeable, but it ships as a fixed serial-console appliance, not a platform you reprogram for other tasks.
price_note: $24.00 direct from termdriver.com (official vendor site). Lab401 sells it as a EUR-converted reseller at roughly $29.95-29.99 (EUR29.00 list, EUR34.95 compare-at).
skill_note: It is a USB-to-serial adapter with a screen; if you already know how to use a UART console, there is nothing new to learn.
build_note: Ready to use over micro-USB; a 0.1" header is also provided for standalone (non-USB) operation as a console.
summary: A USB-to-serial adapter with a built-in 240x240 IPS display that renders the serial stream as a live ANSI terminal, so you can read a device's boot/debug console without a laptop attached. It can also run standalone off header power as a permanent console for an embedded system.
honest_take: This solves a specific annoyance - tailing serial console output without dedicating a laptop screen to a terminal window - and it does that well with real ANSI color and cursor support, not just a scrolling text dump. It is not a logic analyzer, protocol sniffer, or debug probe of any kind: it is a single UART endpoint, full stop, with no SPI, I2C or JTAG/SWD capability at all. At $24 it is priced for the display and RP2040-driven terminal emulation, not for any hacking capability beyond what a $3 USB-UART cable already gives you. If you just need to talk to a serial console with a laptop already open, a bare adapter is cheaper; buy this specifically for the standalone-display use case.
best_for: Watching boot logs / debug console output on a small always-on screen
A standalone serial console for headless embedded systems (e.g. next to a Raspberry Pi)
Reading ANSI-colored terminal output without a laptop attached
not_for: Protocol analysis or sniffing - it is a UART endpoint, not a bus tap
Anything beyond serial - no SPI/I2C/JTAG capability
Situations where a $3 bare USB-UART adapter would already do the job

name: IBDAP - CMSIS-DAP JTAG/SWD Debug Adapter
firmware_note: Official open-source CMSIS-DAP firmware for the LPC11U35 target; the upstream repo shows only 2 commits total, i.e. it was published essentially complete and has not been iterated on since.
price_note: Listed price is $35.95, but the Tindie listing is currently out of stock (schema.org availability: OutOfStock) and the seller's page reads 'this seller is taking a break' with only a restock-notification signup - not a normal temporary sellout.
skill_note: A standard CMSIS-DAP probe - if you already use OpenOCD or Keil with any other CMSIS-DAP adapter, this behaves the same way.
build_note: Ready-to-use USB adapter, no assembly - when it is actually in stock.
summary: An open-hardware CMSIS-DAP debug adapter built on an NXP LPC11U35 Cortex-M0 running at 48 MHz, giving JTAG and SWD access to ARM Cortex targets from multiple vendors (Nordic, Atmel, NXP, Freescale, TI) plus UART/I2C/SPI/ADC/GPIO breakout. Functionally a from-scratch alternative to a DAPLink or ST-Link for Cortex-M debugging, with more general peripheral breakout than most dedicated probes in this comparison.
honest_take: This is a competent, fully open CMSIS-DAP probe on paper, with more peripheral breakout (I2C, dual SPI, 8-channel ADC) than any other debug probe in this batch - but the listing is currently unbuyable. The seller's own page says they are 'taking a break', not just sold out, and the upstream firmware repo has had exactly two commits since it was published, so treat this as effectively dormant rather than an active product. At the price point where this normally sits ($35.95), a Mini DAPLink or an XDS110-class probe from an actively-stocked seller is the safer buy right now; there is nothing IBDAP does for JTAG/SWD that a current CMSIS-DAP probe does not, and its extra peripheral breakout is a bonus you can't currently purchase.
best_for: Historical/reference example of an open CMSIS-DAP design (LPC11U35-based)
Cortex-M debugging via OpenOCD/Keil/GDB/IAR, if you can actually source one
General peripheral breakout (I2C/SPI/ADC/GPIO) alongside debug access, more than most dedicated probes offer
not_for: Buying today - currently unavailable with no restock date
Anyone who needs a probe with an active maintainer
Fault injection or side-channel work - no such hardware

name: Lab401 Flashing Multi-tool for Proxmark & Chameleon
price_note: EUR29.99 (compare-at EUR34.95) direct from lab401.com, converted at time of check to roughly $32.39. KSEC Worldwide sells the same product at GBP34.99. Both are EU/UK-based resellers; check current FX rates.
skill_note: Trivial to use once wired - the whole point is removing the need to solder pogo-pin or wire jigs - but you need to already know how to drive a Segger J-Link or an AVR ISP mkII.
build_note: Solder-free: headers and pins are pre-placed for both target families. No soldering needed on this board itself.
summary: A passive breakout adapter (11 x 8 x 1.5 cm, 8-9 g) that pre-wires the JTAG/ICSP headers needed to reflash a Proxmark 3 RDV4/4.01 or a ChameleonMini RevE/RevG without building your own jig. It is not itself a programmer - it just routes a Segger J-Link (for the Proxmark) or an AVR ISP mkII (for the Chameleon) to the right pins. Intended for brick recovery and switching between major firmware branches; routine firmware updates over USB do not need it.
honest_take: The name overstates what you are buying: this is a header-routing adapter, not a programmer. You still need to separately own a Segger J-Link and/or an AVR ISP mkII - both sold separately and each costing as much or more than this board - before it does anything. Its entire value is saving you from hand-wiring pogo pins to a Proxmark or Chameleon's debug pads, which is a real but narrow convenience specifically for brick recovery and firmware-branch switching (not routine updates, which work fine over USB alone). If you already have proper jigs or don't mind wiring your own, skip it; if you regularly reflash both device families and don't want to fight tiny test points every time, it earns its price.
best_for: Owners of both a Proxmark 3 RDV4 and a ChameleonMini/Tiny who reflash either regularly
Recovering a bricked Proxmark or Chameleon after a failed firmware update
Avoiding hand-soldered pogo-pin jigs for recovery flashing
not_for: Anyone without a Segger J-Link or AVR ISP mkII already - this adapter does nothing on its own
Routine firmware updates - those work over USB without this tool
One-time recovery flashing - a borrowed jig or direct wiring is cheaper for a single use

name: CW312T-RP2350
firmware_note: The board itself ships blank; you load your own test/victim firmware onto the RP2350 via the ChipWhisperer toolchain to build side-channel or fault-injection test targets.
skill_note: This is a target, not a capture tool - using it for real side-channel or glitch work assumes you already know how to run a ChipWhisperer capture session.
build_note: Ready-to-use CW312-format target board; no soldering, but it does nothing on its own.
summary: A CW312-standard target board carrying a Raspberry Pi RP2350 (dual Cortex-M33 + Hazard3 RISC-V), with the chip's internal voltage regulator bypassed in favour of an external LDO so a ChipWhisperer capture unit can cleanly measure and glitch its 1.0 V core supply. It exists purely to give ChipWhisperer owners a current-generation MCU to practice power analysis and fault injection against.
honest_take: This is not a standalone tool - it is a victim board. It plugs into NewAE's CW312 connector standard and needs a separate ChipWhisperer capture device (Nano, Lite or Husky) to do anything at all; budget for that if you don't already own one, since none of the glitching, power-analysis or debug capability lives on this board itself. The value here is specifically that it is a current, real-world MCU family (the RP2350/Pico 2 line) rather than the older toy targets bundled with entry kits, so glitch-detector and power-analysis practice transfers better to real hardware.
best_for: ChipWhisperer owners who want a modern RP2350 target for power analysis practice
Testing glitch-detector circuits against a current-generation MCU
Coursework/training that wants to go beyond the bundled STM32F0/F3 targets
not_for: Anyone without a ChipWhisperer capture device - it has no capture hardware of its own
Attacking a real product's RP2350 - this is a bare dev target, not your product's board

name: teensy4vfi
firmware_note: Bare-metal firmware for the Teensy 4.0/4.1's own NXP i.MX RT1060 chip, turning the board's GPIO into a voltage-glitch trigger/controller. Author explicitly labels the project 'in its very early stages' and a personal exercise in bare-metal SoC programming.
price_note: Not a sold product - the firmware is free. Estimated cost is a bare Teensy 4.0 board, currently $21.49 from SparkFun (which now manufactures Teensy boards); a Teensy 4.1 costs more. You also need whatever crowbar/switching hardware you wire to the target's power rail, which is not included or specified in the repo.
skill_note: The repository ships as raw firmware with almost no documentation ('Docs, readme, measurements, etc.' is listed as an open TODO); you are expected to read and modify the source to use it for a real target.
build_note: Compiles with the ARM GNU Toolchain and a Makefile; flashes to a Teensy 4.0/4.1 with the standard teensy-loader tool. No external hardware requirements are documented in the README, though a real glitch attack on a target chip will need you to wire the Teensy's GPIO to that target's power/reset lines yourself.
summary: Open-source firmware that repurposes a Teensy 4.0/4.1 (an off-the-shelf i.MX RT1060 dev board) as a voltage fault-injection controller, with a Python RPC script for host-side control. It is an early, actively-underdocumented research project rather than a finished glitching tool.
honest_take: The author's own README calls this 'very early stages' and a personal learning project, and that shows: there is no documentation of what external glitch-injection circuit (if any) is needed to actually hit a target's power rail, no measurements, and no published successful attack against a real chip. Compare this squarely against the ChipWhisperer-Nano ($50, ready-to-run with a built-in target and a mature Python/Jupyter course) - that is the safer choice if you are learning voltage glitching for the first time. teensy4vfi is worth watching only if you specifically want to build your own glitcher on hardware you already own and are comfortable filling in the undocumented parts yourself.
best_for: Experienced researchers who want a from-scratch, Teensy-based glitch controller to build on
Learning bare-metal i.MX RT1060 programming alongside fault-injection concepts
not_for: Anyone learning voltage glitching for the first time - use a ChipWhisperer-Nano instead
Reproducible, documented attacks - no measurements or target write-ups are published
Turnkey use - expect to read and patch the source

summary: Open-source firmware that turns dirt-cheap ST-Link v2 clones and STM32 'blue pill' boards into a generic USB JTAG adapter, filling the role of the old LPT Wiggler cable for a few dollars of hardware. It speaks a simple USB protocol (VID 0x1209 / PID 0xC0CA) that UrJTAG, openFPGAloader and flashrom already support natively.
honest_take: The project's own README is refreshingly blunt: 'DirtyJTAG is dirty and dirt cheap, but is not fast nor a perfect implementation of the JTAG protocol.' Independent testing has found its TCK clock effectively capped around 1 MHz no matter what speed you request in software - call it an order of magnitude slower than a real J-Link or even a decent CMSIS-DAP probe. OpenOCD support has existed only as an out-of-tree patch under review rather than a merged feature (check current status before assuming it works out of the box), and the flashy 'runs on a Pi Pico or Tang Nano too' claim is true only via separate community forks, not the official project. It also has no SWD support at all - JTAG only. Buy it for what it is: a way to turn a $2-5 clone board you already have lying around into a slow-but-usable JTAG cable for UrJTAG/openFPGAloader/flashrom, not a fast general debug probe.

honest_take: The headline appeal is the sub-$1 chip, but the CH552's 8051 core is doing everything - CMSIS-DAP framing, SWD/JTAG bit-banging and the USB stack - on an architecture with none of the bit-banging throughput of an ARM Cortex-M0+ (like the RP2040 in a Mini DAPLink) or the LPC11U35 in an IBDAP. It also has no I2C, SPI flash-dumping or glitching capability - it is SWD/JTAG plus UART, nothing more. It is a genuinely good learning project - real open firmware you compile yourself, on real Cortex-M silicon - but not a build you'd choose over a $4.80 pre-assembled Mini DAPLink if raw debugging speed or your own time matters.

name: stm32f1-picopwner
firmware_note: Raspberry Pi Pico firmware implementing a published power-glitch plus Flash Patch and Breakpoint (FPB) attack to bypass STM32F1 Read-Out Protection (RDP) Level 1 and dump flash contents over serial.
price_note: Not a sold product. Estimated cost is a Raspberry Pi Pico (roughly $4-5) plus an ST-Link V2 clone (a few dollars) and the STM32F1 target board itself; the firmware is free.
skill_note: This is a ready-made implementation of a published academic attack, not a beginner tool - you need to wire power, reset, boot and USART lines precisely between the Pico and the target, and understand why the timing-dependent SRAM-retention trick works to troubleshoot it.
build_note: No soldering strictly required (jumper wires to power, reset, BOOT0/BOOT1, and USART TX between the Pico and target board, plus a pull-up resistor on BOOT1), but precise wiring and an ST-Link V2 for the initial setup phase are required.
summary: A ready-to-run implementation, on a $4 Raspberry Pi Pico, of a published academic power-glitch attack that bypasses STM32F1 Read-Out Protection Level 1 by keeping exploit code alive in SRAM across a power cycle, then using the Flash Patch and Breakpoint unit to redirect execution and dump the protected flash over serial.
honest_take: This turns a peer-reviewed, previously-manual RDP bypass into something you can run with a Pico and some jumper wires, which is genuinely valuable - but know its limits before relying on it. It only affects RDP Level 1 (not Level 2, which is designed to be unrecoverable), and the technique is reported to have been closed in STM32F1 silicon revisions from 2020 onward, so it will not work against a current-production chip. It is also STM32F1-specific - it has no JTAG/SWD debugging function of its own beyond the exploit's use of an external ST-Link, and no I2C or general bus-probe capability. Treat this as a tool for older STM32F1 stock or legacy-device forensics, not a general 'unlock any STM32' button - and note the repo carries no explicit license, so redistribution terms are unclear.

not_for: RDP Level 2 - not affected by this or any known glitch bypass
Current-production STM32F1 chips - reportedly patched in revisions from 2020 onward
Any STM32 family other than F1 - this targets F1-specific RDP behaviour
General-purpose debugging - it is a single exploit, not a debug probe

name: Mini DAPLink Debug Probe
firmware_note: Vendor states source code and documentation are available on GitHub; specific repo URL not published on the listing.
price_note: $4.80 for the base unit on Tindie, in stock (64 units). Kits with DuPont cables or a bundled 1m USB-C cable are also offered. This is the cheapest debug probe in this batch.
skill_note: Standard driverless CMSIS-DAP operation with Keil/IAR/pyOCD/OpenOCD - if you've used any DAPLink-class probe before, this behaves the same way.
build_note: Tiny cased USB-C dongle, no assembly.
summary: A 3.2 x 1.7 cm USB-C CMSIS-DAP/DAPLink probe for ARM Cortex-M targets (STM32, GD32, nRF51/52) over SWD or JTAG, with a built-in UART bridge that enumerates as a serial port alongside the debug interface. At $4.80 it is the budget floor of the debug-probe market covered in this batch, and the same MuseLab store also sells a 'Mini High-Speed DAPLink' variant, implying this base model is the slower of the two.
honest_take: This is the price-to-performance benchmark every other probe in this batch has to be measured against: $4.80 for a driverless, CMSIS-DAP-compliant SWD/JTAG probe plus a UART bridge is genuinely hard to beat, and it is built on the same DAPLink lineage as far more expensive branded probes. The vendor's claim of being faster than J-Link/ST-Link at a lower price is a marketing line from the Tindie listing, not something independently benchmarked here - mark it as claimed, not confirmed, and note that MuseLab sells a separate 'Mini High-Speed DAPLink' as a different product, which quietly suggests this base model is not the fast option in their own lineup. Its real limitation next to the IBDAP or XDS110 in this batch is scope: it is SWD/JTAG-plus-UART only, with no I2C/SPI/ADC breakout or glitching, so it is a pure debug probe rather than a general peripheral-access tool.
